rules.why: A list of text is written in two different ways and the rule names one. An array of texts is written on ONE line as double-quoted items joined by commas (line 164), and an empty array as 'None'. A list of texts (List) is written in brackets, one double-quoted item per line (165-171), and an empty List is written as an empty bracket pair, not 'None'. The rule's 'An empty list is written as None' and 'A list of text is written in brackets' each hold for only one of the two. Say which value shape gets which form.

The description of git's text ('a tag, commit count and short commit name when tags exist, and a short commit name otherwise') rests on how git describe behaves, which the script does not show; it also omits that on a commit that is exactly tagged the text is the tag alone. State what the lines show (the script writes the output of 'git describe --always' as the version text) and put the detail of that output in an assumed Fact, or drop it. The script also rewrites the whole generated file (line 3 overwrites, 4-8 append), not just the version.

The code restores the remembered position when it is still inside the list (index below the count), not 'if the result is still in the list': nothing checks that the same policy is there. Reword to position, which is what a rebuilder must keep.

The rule refuses the template at line 44, before its items are staged (lines 72-77), so it governs the same staging transition (transition-86521319960986518382) as the other refusal rules of the job (unparsable template, namespace already owned, missing language file), which all gate it. It has no gates, which the checklist counts as a defect. Add the gates to that transition. Say too that templates read before the faulty one stay staged but unbuilt, so that a later load builds them.

Two decisions in one rule, and the second is owned by the wrong block: Open File (3-10) and Reset (36-40, a block of its own, given here only as evidence). Split into a rule for Open File decided at 3-10 (whole file replaces typed text without asking) and a rule for Reset decided at 36-40 (needs a Yes to the question, then restores the header). 'Without checking it' is the weakness in fact-44356108302568422603; do not repeat it inside the rule.

The value term is passed to Like, which also gives meaning to # (any digit) and [..] character lists, not only * and ?. Saying only * and ? are wildcards is short of the reach, and a value term with [ or # behaves differently from plain text even with no * or ?. State that the value term is always a Like pattern (so # and [ ] also act), as the fact on malformed patterns already relies on.

The reach is now right, but 'each with a Registry.pol path' is false for a POL file source: its path is whatever file the person typed or browsed to (line 39, OpenPol.vb browse filter is *.pol), not a Registry.pol; only the local and per-user Group Policy have a Registry.pol path (lines 18, 41). Say: a POL file at the path given, the local Group Policy and a per-user Group Policy at their Registry.pol.

'A definition with no entries, or none met, is met only when all are required' is false for 'none met'. When all are required (requireAll) the first unmet entry returns False at 408 or 416, so a definition with entries and none met is never met; when not required, no entry met falls to line 421 and returns False. Only a definition with NO entries is met, and only when all are required (421 returns the flag). Correct the clause to the empty case alone.

Two things are in one rule: the not-found/blank icon outcome (holds) and the stale section left over from an earlier match. The stale section is a weakness (lines 24-27 clear policy, category, product and support but not SelectedSection; it is reset only on a policy match, 44-48) and belongs in its own fact with a risk, not inside a rule. Keep the rule to the icon outcome and write the weakness as a fact.

'Writes every option whatever its value, including options never filled in' overreaches: a drop-down option with no choice is not written, line 264 fails and the apply stops (fact-21033848734857416942), and an unopened list option is written with no list (fact-56821189303055742863). Say that every option is read and written whatever its value, except that an unchosen drop-down stops the apply.

Two different weaknesses and a rule are merged in one record: an unclosed opening quote drops the phrase silently, and a one-word quoted term such as "abc" never closes itself (the branch at 42-43 does not test for an ending quote) so it absorbs the following words up to the next word ending in a quote, or is dropped with them. The previous review asked for the unclosed-quote weakness as its own finding; it is still only inside a rule. Keep the rule as how a phrase is read, and write each weakness as its own fact with its lines and a risk.

The rule now says deletion entries are lost and that "values of sub-keys are not put back", and that Clear everything "removes all values". Both mislead a rebuild. ClearKey (PolicySource.vb 183-186) forgets only the values listed directly under the key (GetValueNames matches the key plus the value separator, so entries of sub-keys do not match); values of sub-keys are never removed, so there is nothing to put back and they stay as they were. Say that the clearing removes (and marks cleared) only the key itself, its direct values including any deletion entries and its empty-key marker, and that sub-keys keep their values, rather than that sub-key values are lost or not restored. The rest of the rule (OK refused until a choice, empty name message, ordinary values only put back, deletion entry replacing any value of that name) holds.

The second sentence is false for this stub. PolFile.ApplyDifference calls only DeleteValue, ClearKey, SetValue and ForgetValue on the target (157-170, 176); it never asks the target checking whether a value will be deleted. So applying a policy file to a REG file does not fail through this routine; only ForgetValue (RegFile 237-239, reached at PolicySource 176) does. Either drop the claim from this rule, or drop the rule: a stub that throws and is never reached by the REG flows decides nothing a rebuilder needs. Keep the consequence on the ForgetValue rule and the existing fact.

'The defined on or off value is then saved ... and overwrites the first step' is not what the lines show. The first step (lines 317-322) runs only when the checkbox has NO defined on value (ticked) or NO defined off value (unticked), and in that case setList (323) has no main value to write, so nothing overwrites the 1 or the removal. The two are alternatives for the main value, not a sequence. Only an extra value listed for that state can touch the same value name. Rewrite: with no defined main value the default applies (1 when ticked, removal when unticked); with one, that value is saved; the extra values for the state are saved in both cases.

The rule says the workspace 'stays empty' also when the load fails after the person chose Yes. The workspace is emptied at line 65 (and again at 72) but is not reset in the inner Catch (74-76); a load that fails after some definition files were added would leave a partly filled workspace. The lines do not show whether LoadFolder can fail after adding files, so say 'the workspace is not reset again after that failure' or confirm it from the loader before claiming it is empty.

The new wording says the accepted edit dialog changes the open policy source 'in memory only' and that nothing is written until Save Policies. That holds for POL-file-backed sources only. A registry source writes the edit to the registry at once (its save reports 'already applied', PolicyLoader.vb:134-135), and a loaded user hive file is written into the mounted hive and applied when closed (137). Restrict the memory-only and nothing-on-disk clauses to POL-file-backed sources and name the registry case, as the rule on opening sources already does. Keep the two refresh branches.

The last sentence says a negative number kept where the minimum is below zero 'is converted to an unsigned number when applied'. Line 251 is CUInt of the box text; the code does not show a conversion, and converting a negative text to an unsigned integer may instead fail, which would stop the apply after line 242 has already cleared the policy (the same effect fact-21033848734857416942 names). Either state it as unsettled (an assumed Fact, rules-it-applies, confirmed by runningSystem: what a negative value does at line 251) or drop the word 'converted' and say only that the negative text is passed to an unsigned conversion whose result the code does not show.

The second sentence is false for this stub. PolFile.ApplyDifference calls only DeleteValue, ClearKey, SetValue and ForgetValue on the target (157-170, 176); it never asks the target reading a value. So applying a policy file to a REG file does not fail through this routine; only ForgetValue (RegFile 237-239, reached at PolicySource 176) does. Either drop the claim from this rule, or drop the rule: a stub that throws and is never reached by the REG flows decides nothing a rebuilder needs. Keep the consequence on the ForgetValue rule and the existing fact.

'For any other kind of setting the empty value makes the write fail' is not shown for every kind. The project is built with Option Strict Off (PolicyPlus.vbproj line 49), so the stored Nothing is converted loosely: a number setting not stored as text goes through CUInt(Nothing) (line 312) and writes 0; a checkbox takes Nothing as unticked (316), saving its off state; a dropdown indexes its items with Nothing (349), which converts to position 0 and picks the first item. Only text-type and multi-line settings visibly hand Nothing to the writer (310, 327, 353), and whether that fails is decided in the POL/registry writer, not here. State what the person ends up with per kind (list: entries cleared unless others are kept; number, checkbox, dropdown: a default value is written), or limit the claim to what the lines prove.

The second sentence is false for this stub. PolFile.ApplyDifference calls only DeleteValue, ClearKey, SetValue and ForgetValue on the target (157-170, 176); it never asks the target listing a key's values. So applying a policy file to a REG file does not fail through this routine; only ForgetValue (RegFile 237-239, reached at PolicySource 176) does. Either drop the claim from this rule, or drop the rule: a stub that throws and is never reached by the REG flows decides nothing a rebuilder needs. Keep the consequence on the ForgetValue rule and the existing fact.

The clause 'a policy's category or supported-on reference' can be read as a policy that has no parent-category or supported-on entry. Such a policy is not refused by the file load: the file loads and the failure comes later, when the structures are built (AdmxBundle.vb:153 and 159 read the missing reference), which is the case the build-failure finding states. Only an entry that is present without its reference is refused here (AdmxFile.vb:191, 193). Write it as 'a policy's parent-category or supported-on entry without a reference' so a tester does not expect a refusal for a policy with no entry.

The second sentence is false for this stub. PolFile.ApplyDifference calls only DeleteValue, ClearKey, SetValue and ForgetValue on the target (157-170, 176); it never asks the target asking whether a value is present. So applying a policy file to a REG file does not fail through this routine; only ForgetValue (RegFile 237-239, reached at PolicySource 176) does. Either drop the claim from this rule, or drop the rule: a stub that throws and is never reached by the REG flows decides nothing a rebuilder needs. Keep the consequence on the ForgetValue rule and the existing fact.
